1:
The Syrian general is introduced with a break from what precedes, and Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) will not fix the reign, saying only that it was a time of peace; he glosses the name as a title of the sun-god and draws attention to the high prophetic view that it is Jehovah, and not Hadad or Rimmon, who gives victory to Syria as well as to Israel. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reports that Jarchi and others identify him with the man who drew the bow at a venture and killed Ahab, and finds it strange that Josephus passes him over when the history stands in the Chaldee, the Septuagint and the Syriac; Ellicott credits the same identification to the Midrash. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) presses the point from the other side: the prosperity even of those who do not know God must be ascribed to him, and Israel should know that when the Syrians prevailed it was from the Lord.

The leprosy is read as the flaw in the greatness. Henry holds that no man’s honour or valour can set him out of reach of the sorest calamities, there being many a sickly body under gay clothing, and that every man has some but that diminishes him — quoting Bishop Hall, that the basest slave in Syria would not change skins with him. Clarke makes it a providential rule, that God often permits great defects to accompany great eminence in order to hide pride from man. Ellicott renders the clause as a brave warrior stricken with leprosy, and notes the irony Thenius found in it, that the victor over Israel must seek and find his only help in Israel.

The captive maid draws the warmest comment. Clarke infers pious parents who had taught her the true God, sets the goodness of providence against its severity — affectionate parents robbed of a promising daughter by freebooters — and answers himself: if God allowed the parents to lose the child, he did not allow the child to be without a guardian. By her captivity one of the most considerable families in Syria was brought to the knowledge of God. Henry makes the rule that the unhappy dispersing of God’s people has sometimes been the happy occasion of spreading the knowledge of God, and notes that no leper had yet been cleansed in Israel, so that she inferred the power from his other miracles and the willingness from his kindness. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) explain the idiom for receiving a man back from leprosy from the reception of Miriam into the camp.

The present is counted differently. Clarke reckons the silver and gold at better than fourteen thousand pounds besides the raiment, and calls it princely; Keil and Delitzsch take the figures as they stand and judge the sum in keeping with the man’s position and not too great for the cure of a malady that would certainly prove fatal. Ellicott works out the same amounts, renders the raiment as holiday suits, and concludes that the total appears much too large and the numbers are probably corrupt, as is so often the case.

On the king’s alarm all four agree it was unbelief, and divide only on what he feared. John Gill (reformed) and Ellicott have him rend his clothes as at blasphemy, Ellicott adding that leprosy was a kind of living death. Clarke has him reason from the maxim, held in Syria as in Israel, that God alone can cure the disease, and so infer a quarrel. Henry sees both an affront to God and a design on himself, and says the fright came of misreading a letter well intended — it is charity to ourselves to think no evil — the king having made himself such a stranger to the prophet that the captive maid had Elisha more in her thoughts than he had.
9:
Why the prophet would not come to the door divides the witnesses six ways. John Gill (reformed) has him retired as he commonly was, perhaps at prayer, and willing besides to show his contempt of worldly grandeur and to mortify the visitor’s pride. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) allows either reason: devotion he would not be diverted from, or a lesson that before the great God all men stand on the same level. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) says simply that he had his orders from God and passed them on by a servant. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) makes it partly a trial of faith and obedience, partly a point of honour for his religion, that he might be seen to seek God’s glory and not his own. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) rule out three explanations by name — the legal bar on dealings with lepers, which Ephraem Syrus assumes, fear of the leper, which Thenius suggests, and a wish to magnify the miracle, which C. a Lapide imagines — and put it down to the man’s own state of mind. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) returns to avoiding contact with a leper, noting that once cleansed the man goes in and stands before the prophet, and rejects the pride reading outright: Thenius is right that there is no trace of pride about Naaman.

The state he arrived in is noticed by all. Gill takes the retinue for his own grandeur and the prophet’s honour both; Ellicott reads the plural as suggesting magnificence, and will not have it, with Bähr, that the house was a hovel he disdained to enter. Clarke is blunter: inspected closely the thing was preposterous, a leper sitting in state and affecting it. Henry turns it into the posture of a suppliant: those who showed prophets little respect at other times were complaisant enough when they needed them, and this one waited at the door as a beggar waits for an alms.

That the river was a sign and not a medicine, three of them are careful to establish. Henry denies it was any means of cure at all: cold bathing may be wholesome in general, but in a leprosy some think it rather hurtful, so the washing was a sign and a trial of obedience: those who will be helped of God must do as they are bidden. Clarke grants the water no tendency to remove the disorder and makes it a doctrine: the author of life and health may convey them by what means he pleases. Ellicott says the command itself made clear that no external application of the prophet’s was curing anything, quoting Bähr that Syrians knew as well as Israelites that the Jordan could not heal leprosy. Keil and Delitzsch add why the flesh is said to return: the leprosy had turned it to festering matter.

The rage is anatomised most closely by Clarke, who breaks the complaint into four expectations: that the prophet would come out in person rather than make a servant the go-between; that he would stand as a servant waiting on the orders of his God; that he would call on his God’s name, so that God and prophet together should appear to do him honour; and that he would strike his hand over the place, since how should healing virtue be conveyed without contact? Henry finds in the laid scheme the folly of pride: the man forgot that he was a leper, who ought not to stand on punctilios of honour, and a petitioner besides, and beggars must not be choosers. Ellicott corrects the gesture to a waving of the hand toward the place, since the prophet would not touch what was unclean, and declines Thenius’s rendering of the last phrase as the leprous part. Wesley puts it in four words: he supposed himself despised.
12:
The two rivers of Damascus are identified three ways. John Gill (reformed) takes the first from the marginal Amana and Mount Amana in Syria, equates it with the Chrysorrhoas of Pliny, and makes the second the Orontes that runs by the walls of Antioch; he adds that no trace of either name survives, the only river at Damascus now being the Barrady, which Maundrell describes dividing into three streams. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) will not identify them at all, Maundrell having travelled the whole ground and found no vestige of the names, but supposes two branches of the Barrady must be meant, called Barda and Toura by the time the Arabic version was made. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) is confident of both: the first is the present Burâda, the cold, descending from Anti-Lebanon through Damascus in seven streams, the second the Nahr el-Awâj, the swift, coming down from the great Hermon to pass south of the city. He alone draws the contrast that gives the complaint its force: both are clear mountain water, where the Jordan is turbid and discoloured.

To the question whether he might not as well wash at home, three answer. Clarke answers flatly no, since God had directed him to Jordan and by its waters or none should he be cleansed: the two rivers may be as good, and the whole difference is that God will convey his influence by the one and not the other — a contention common enough among men, the Ganges bearing the bell in Bengal as the Thames does in England. Ellicott makes the same point from the other end: if mere washing in a river were enough, it were easy to do that at home and to much better advantage. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) grants the rivers equal virtue as water and says what the man should have considered, that the cure was not to be wrought by the water but by the power of God.

On the servants’ address there is a fourfold difference. Gill denies it is familiar or affectionate at all and makes it a term of honour and submission, rendering it my lord with the Targum; Clarke calls it a title of the highest respect and affection; Wesley reads it as our father, spoken to show reverence and affection together; Ellicott allows the title but floats the possibility that the word is not a title but a corruption of the particle for if, which the Hebrew does not otherwise express. Their argument is set out by Clarke — had something difficult and costly been required you would have done it, so much the more what costs nothing — and Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) notes who delivered it: a great mercy to have those about us who will tell us our faults though they are our inferiors.

The obedience, when it came, was grudging. Henry observes that he was bidden to wash seven times and did but dip himself as many times, as lightly as he could, yet God so far honoured his own word as to make even that effectual. Clarke has him make the trial expecting little, and then finds the scurf entirely gone and the flesh of a youth in its place. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) explain the number as the stamp of the works of God, and Ellicott, quoting them, adds the covenant with Israel on which the cure depended — then sets beside it a parallel from the Assyrian exorcism texts of the age of Sargon of Agadê, where Merodach asks his father Hea how a sick man may be cured and is told to send him to bathe in the sacred waters at the mouth of the Euphrates — so that the command fell in with an ancient Semitic belief about the healing virtue of running streams.
15:
The confession is weighed two ways. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) takes it for a noble one, which exposes the misery of the Gentile world, since nations that had many gods really had none; and the mercy of the cure moved the man more than its miracle, those being best able to speak of divine grace who have felt it. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) hears less: like most contemporaries, Jewish as well as Syrian, the man believed in locally restricted deities, and in concluding that there is no god save in Israel he keeps that conception intact — which Ellicott calls a mark of historic truth in the account.

On the refused present they agree in substance and differ in reason. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) have him avoid all appearance of the selfishness that moved the false prophets; Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian), that the Syrians might take a gift for payment of a cure God alone had worked; John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) that they should see how God’s servants despised the wealth the prophets of the Gentiles sought so greedily. Henry denies that the prophet did not need it, being poor enough, or thought it unlawful, having taken presents from others: he would not have this Syrian able to say he had made Elisha rich.

What the two mules’ burden was splits them. John Gill (reformed), Ellicott and Henry read it as earth for an altar: Gill reports Jewish writers who have him ask for soil from the prophet’s own house, conceiving a holiness in the ground he trod; Ellicott finds it natural to a local idea of divinity; Henry calls it an over-doing to match the earlier under-valuing, the man who slighted the waters of Israel now over-valuing its earth, and likens the wish to asking a man for his picture. Clarke and Wesley both reject this. Clarke asks why leave was needed for earth he could lift anywhere, and how an altar could be built of two mules’ load carried to Damascus; he takes the burden for the silver and gold, called earth as others call gold thick clay, and leaves the reader to choose. Wesley says the same and asks what altar two mules could carry into Syria, unless they were as large and strong as elephants.

The reservation about the house of Rimmon divides them again. Henry allows the plea might admit of some apology, the man owning he ought not and pleading his place at court, yet turns it on the reader: a reservation for any known sin is a defeasance of the covenant. Clarke will not have the plea at all, holding that by no rule of reasoning can the man be asking pardon for what he may yet commit, since that would be the doctrine of indulgences; he reads the verbs in the past with Lightfoot, so the pardon sought is for bowings already done. Ellicott takes it as a prayer for an unavoidable exception, apparent rather than real, not to be judged by a Christian standard.

What the dismissal conceded is disputed four ways. Ellicott holds that the prophet, as spokesman of Jehovah, acceded to the prayer. Keil and Delitzsch hold that he neither approved nor disapproved, since no permission had been asked and without a special command he could only commend a new convert to God’s guidance; most earlier theologians, they note, found a direct approval in the words. Clarke’s past-tense reading makes the question not arise, and he reports a marginal note in one of De Rossi’s manuscripts directing that the word be read not rather than to him — on which the answer becomes a refusal, and the sense is that he keep his resolutions and avoid all idolatry. Ellicott identifies the god as the Assyrian thunderer of the air, identified with Hadad, of whom the tablets yield forty-one titles.
20:
Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) and John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) open on the same contrast in nearly the same words: one would have expected a prophet’s servant to be a saint, yet the best ministers have often had about them those who were their grief and shame. Henry sharpens it: the Syrian soldier had many servants and they were wise and good, the holy prophet has one and he proves a liar; those who heard of Elisha at a distance got good by it, while the man who stood continually before him took no impression, for the means of grace cannot give grace. On the motive they agree it was money: Henry calls it the root of all evil and quotes Bishop Hall, that the man’s heart was packed up in the Syrian’s chests and he must run to fetch it. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) finds the self-justification in the words, the servant reasoning on the principle of spoiling the Egyptians; Wesley adds that the oath was sworn to give the deed a pretence, not considering that swearing to do a wicked thing does not excuse it but makes it worse.

Henry anatomises the lie. The claim that his master sent him was deliberate, and it diverted to himself the courtesy meant for the prophet; worse, it painted Elisha as a man who had repented of his own generosity, who would say and unsay, swear and unswear. The tale of two young scholars from the hill-country Henry calls as silly as it was false, since if a token were wanted for two of them, less than a talent of silver might have served. And he weighs what it risked: the convert might have concluded, as Paul’s enemies said of him, that the master kept his hands clean and sent others to make a gain of him, which might have driven him back to his idols — so Henry hopes he learnt in time that Elisha had no part in it.

The Syrian’s conduct is the foil to it. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) have him spring down the moment he sees the servant running, in reverential gratitude toward the prophet, and then press two talents on a man who had asked for one, sending two of his own servants to carry them ahead. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) marks that he treats even a servant with the profoundest respect, and renders his greeting as an asking after peace. Ellicott calls the descent an Oriental mark of respect and reads haste in the idiom, adding that the man feared something had befallen the prophet; Wesley notes that the gift was pressed on one who first declined it under a pretence of modesty. Clarke supplies the weight that made the two bearers necessary, each talent running to some hundred and twenty pounds.

Where the goods were hidden is read three ways. John Gill (reformed) takes it for a fortified post at Samaria with a watch, to whom the money could safely be committed. Clarke follows the Chaldee, Greek, Syriac and Arabic in making the word a secret or dark place, and draws the moral that a man doing a deed of darkness sought darkness to hide it in. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch make it the mound of the city — Ellicott allowing either the rise on which the prophet’s house stood, where no window would have overlooked their approach, or a fortified hill among the defences of Samaria like the Ophel at Jerusalem, and remarking that so particular a note of place is itself a note of historical truth. Henry adds the sacrilege: the man hid his gain as Achan hid his, then stood before his master ready for orders, none looking more observant and none more injurious, applauding a fraud he thought had deceived the prophet as Ananias and Sapphira thought to deceive the apostles.
25:
The prophet’s question about his heart is the hardest clause here, and has been read five ways. John Gill (reformed) lays out three from the Jewish commentators: that his knowledge had not departed, so nothing could be hidden, which he credits to Ben Gersom; that his heart did not go with the errand, the deed being against his will, which he credits to Abendana; and the Targum’s, that the matter was shown him by a spirit of prophecy, to which he adds Maimonides. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) will allow only one — that his heart had gone when the man turned from his chariot — calling it the only correct reading of words explained very differently elsewhere, and noting that Theodoret and the Vulgate had given it already, and that it agrees in sense with Thenius, who has the prophet present in spirit. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) reaches the same sense and adds the point that makes it bite: the prophet adopts his servant’s own phrase in severe irony. He observes too that the English follows the Greek in supplying with thee, which the Hebrew lacks.

On the rebuke, Ellicott weighs a variant first. Pointed differently the Hebrew yields a statement rather than a question, as the Greek, the Vulgate and the Arabic take it, but he judges the Masoretic pointing much more suitable and renders the sense: was that of all occasions the time to yield to gain, when the man dealt with was a heathen, who ought rather to have learnt not to confound the prophets of Jehovah with the diviners of the false gods? Keil and Delitzsch read the list of silver, clothes, oliveyards, flocks and slaves as the question’s substance, and Ellicott takes it for a disclosure of what the servant meant to buy. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) puts it sharpest: could he find no better way of getting money than by belying his master and laying a stumbling-block before a young convert?

The sentence is read as an exchange. Henry has it that if he will have the money he must take the disease with it, and that a man contriving to entail lands entailed a loathsome disease instead. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) says the same in a sentence — he had the Syrian’s silver and should have the Syrian’s leprosy — and adds that the white spot appeared as the curse was spoken. How long the curse ran they dispute. Clarke reports an opinion that descendants of his are leprous still, says Maundrell inquired in Judea and could not establish it, and calls it absurd, since the sentence held only until the posterity became extinct, which under such a disease must have come soon; John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) reads the phrase as some generations, and notes that the white sort was reckoned by physicians the worst and incurable. Ellicott answers the objection that the sentence is too severe: the prophet pronounces inspired judgment, milder language might have left a false impression, and covetousness and lying are never spared in Scripture — which he thinks well for mankind.

Clarke closes by reading the chapter as a single providence: a raiding party was permitted the borders, a girl was carried off, she came into the Syrian’s house and waited on his wife, named the God of Israel and his prophet, and her master travelled on the strength of what she said, was healed, and acknowledged the Lord with, as Clarke supposes, his whole household. What was severe to her parents was kindness to that family, and they lost their child only for a time; the frowning providence, in the line he quotes, hid a smiling face behind it. And he draws the lesson he thinks the story exists to teach: without a religious education the girl could never have been the instrument of so great a deliverance.
